rows.R: Protocol v5.0 p.43 (§10.1.1) says each painTRAINER session takes 45-60 min and p.44 says coach sessions take 60 min; main p.3 and TIDieR Supp3 pp.3-4 give 30-45 min (online) and 45-60 min (coach). Real plan-report difference in described session dose; whether content changed or only the time estimate is not stated, so L indeterminate.
rows.evidence: Main p.3 (text layer); protocol Supp1 pp.43-44 (garbled text layer; OCR, then rendered at 120 dpi and read); TIDieR Supp3 pp.3-4 (text layer).
rows.rationale: Protocol v5.0 (10 Nov 2022) §10.1.1: 'Each session takes 45-60 minutes to complete'; §10.1.2: coach sessions take 60 minutes. Article p.3: painTRAINER sessions require 'approximately 30 to 45 minutes'; coach sessions 'lasted about 45 to 60 minutes'. TIDieR Procedures repeats 30-45 and 45-60. Both online endpoints differ by 15 minutes. The article's coach wording ('lasted') reads as observed duration, while the online wording is an expected completion time; the protocol gives design durations. Codebook protocol_report covers planned versus reported conduct, so a different stated per-session dose is within scope even though it is not an analysis element. I cannot tell whether the program content changed or whether the estimate was revised, hence L indeterminate. Card read after judgment; it treats the coach range as context only, whereas I note the coach range also differs (60 vs 45-60); no change to the decision.

rows.R: Main p.4: painTRAINER '371 (43%) completed at least 6 sessions'; Figure 1 (p.5) gives 776 randomized, 371/156/249 completing 6-8/1-5/0 sessions. 371/776 = 47.8% (printed 43%). Neighbors reproduce: 527/776 = 67.9% (68%), 548/778 = 70.4% (70%), 660/778 = 84.8% (85%).
rows.evidence: Main pp.4-5 (text layer; Figure 1 text read).
rows.rationale: The adherence sentence and Figure 1 refer to the same randomized painTRAINER group (n=776). 371/776 = 47.81%; no plausible alternative denominator gives 43% (371/863 would be needed). All other adherence and follow-up percentages in the paragraph reproduce from Figure 1 counts (527/776 = 67.9%, 548/778 = 70.4%, 660/778 = 84.8%, 643/776 = 82.9%, 690/778 = 88.7%, 703/777 = 90.5%, 3-month 542/776 = 69.8%, 635/778 = 81.6%, 621/777 = 79.9%). Confirmed percentage error. Minor because the count is correct and the true value is derivable; J possible because the therapeutic-dose adherence proportion is the kind of process figure that is quoted or pooled, and the error understates painTRAINER adherence by about 5 points. Card read after judgment; agrees.

rows.R: Main p.4 and Table 3 footnote d define SMD = adjusted MD / SD of change in usual care at that time, so within a row the three SMDs share one SD. For 19 of 21 rows (pp.10-11) no single SD reproduces all three SMDs from the printed MDs within rounding; 4 SMDs have the opposite sign to their MD (eg physical 3 mo HC vs UC MD 0.7, SMD -0.02). Text p.7 also cites 3-month SMDs -0.26/-0.36, which are the 6-month values.
rows.evidence: Main pp.4, 7, 10-11 (text layer plus 200-dpi renders of pp.10-11); R script smd_check.R.
rows.rationale: Recomputation (R): for each of the 21 outcome/time rows I searched SD in 0.3-30 for a value making all three |MD+/-0.05|/SD intervals overlap the printed SMD+/-0.005; only pain intensity 6 and 12 months admit a common SD. The card's additive identity (SMD_HC-UC = SMD_PT-UC + SMD_HC-PT under a common denominator) fails in 17 rows and scaling fails in 3 more; my test and the card agree that 20 rows are incompatible. Sign reversals (MD vs SMD): physical 3 mo HC-UC 0.7 vs -0.02; physical 6 mo HC-PT -0.3 vs 0.22; physical 12 mo HC-PT -0.1 vs 0.27; PGIC-pain 12 mo HC-PT 0.1 vs -0.29. HC-PT SMDs of -0.11 to -0.13 with MD 0.0 are impossible for the SDs implied by the PT-UC column (about 1.4-1.9 for pain scores). The social and physical SMD columns look misassigned between contrasts (HC-UC, with the largest MD, has the smallest SMD). This is not rounding. Beyond the card: the Results text (p.7) gives 3-month SMDs -0.26 (painTRAINER) and -0.36 (health coach), but Table 3 prints -0.25 and -0.34 at 3 months and -0.26/-0.36 at 6 months. Substantive and direct: SMDs are the effect sizes a meta-analyst would extract, and both magnitudes and signs are unreliable. Card read after judgment; consistent.

rows.R: NNT points are consistently rounded up (ceiling), the usual NNT convention: ceiling of 100/(difference in printed adjusted %) reproduces all 57 positive NNT points in Table 2 (main p.9) and eTables 7-8 (Supp4 pp.11, 14) within display rounding, whereas round-to-nearest fails 22 of 57. The three flagged cells (8, 7, 8) fit ceiling (7.04->8, 6.02->7, 7.04->8). Convention unstated but explains the pattern.
rows.evidence: Main pp.4, 9 (text layer and 200-dpi render); Supp4 pp.11, 14 (text layer); R script nnt_round.R.
rows.rationale: NNT is defined as 1 over the difference in adjusted percentages (p.4, Table 2 footnote d). For each cell I allowed +/-0.05 on both percentages (RD +/-0.1 points) and asked whether nearest-integer or ceiling rounding of 100/RD can give the printed integer. Table 2: ceiling 27/27, nearest 18/27; eTables 7-8: ceiling 30/30, nearest 17/30. Cells failing nearest but fitting ceiling include several not flagged (eg severity 12-mo PT/UC 11.36 -> 12; intensity 3-mo PT/UC 15.15 -> 16; complete-case 3-mo PT/UC 12.20 -> 13). The flagged cells are 37.1-22.9 = 14.2 -> 7.04 -> 8; 40.9-24.3 = 16.6 -> 6.02 -> 7; 35.6-21.3 = 14.3 -> 6.99, with input rounding 6.94-7.04 -> ceiling 7 or 8. A uniform round-up rule (standard for NNTs so that the benefit is not overstated) explains every point, so the apparent nonreproduction is not an error. The paper does not state the rounding rule, a minor omission I do not treat as a finding. The card lists upward rounding as an alternative; my full-table check shows it is the operative convention.

rows.R: Protocol §15.5 (p.56) and SAP v6.0 §14 (p.20) list prespecified primary covariates as baseline pain severity, sex, site, rural/underserved residence, multisite pain and mental-health condition (no age), as does main p.4; Supp4 p.4, eTable 2 (p.7) and workbook eTable 3 (G10 'X') call age >=65 part of the prespecified base set, and age is fitted in eTables 3-5.
rows.evidence: Protocol Supp1 p.56 (rendered); SAP Supp2 pp.20-21 (OCR, then rendered); main p.4; Supp4 pp.4, 7-10 (text layer); Supp5 xlsx sheet 'eTable 3' cells G2, A10, G10 (openpyxl).
rows.rationale: Both plans name six fixed adjustment factors without age; SAP §13 lists age only among candidate baseline variables and subgroups. The report fits age in the imputation, estimation and weight models and describes it as part of the 'base set of pre-specified adjustment variables', and the workbook marks age as a prespecified adjustment variable. The covariate set of the primary model therefore differs from the plan by age, and the report's prespecification claim has no basis in the supplied plan versions (protocol v5.0, SAP v6.0). The main article's list matches the plan, so the report is also internally inconsistent about age. Retained as a plan-report difference in the primary analysis covariates. Card read after judgment; agrees.

rows.R: Protocol §15.6 (p.57) and SAP §15 (p.21): secondary analyses adjust for baseline pain severity and all stratification variables. Main p.4: secondary outcomes use the primary model structure (adding multisite pain, mental-health condition) plus the baseline value of each secondary outcome. Covariate set differs from plan.
rows.evidence: Protocol Supp1 p.57 (rendered); SAP Supp2 p.21 (rendered); main p.4, Table 3 pp.10-11.
rows.rationale: The plans say secondary analyses follow the Aim 1 approach but then specify the covariates as baseline pain severity and stratification variables. The report adjusts additionally for the given baseline secondary outcome and, through the primary structure, for multisite pain and mental-health condition. Adjusting for the outcome's own baseline is standard and arguably an improvement, but it is a change in the analysis model. For the PGIC outcomes, which have no baseline measurement, the stated baseline adjustment is unclear, and Table 3 labels PGIC as 'mean change from baseline' (observed, outside the candidate). Card read after judgment; agrees.

rows.R: SAP v6.0 §11 (p.19): 'For the primary analyses, we will analyze those patients who have follow-up data' under MAR; pattern-mixture plus IPW is the 'first approach' when missingness >15%, worst/best case the sensitivity analysis. Report (main p.4; Supp4 pp.4-5, eTables 4 and 7) makes MNAR pattern-mixture with IPW the primary analysis and labels complete-case a 'pre-specified sensitivity analysis'. IPW added by 17 Jul 2024 amendment (SAP p.4), after follow-up ended; disclosed Supp4 p.5.
rows.evidence: SAP Supp2 pp.4, 19 (garbled text layer; OCR and 130-dpi render read); main p.4; Supp4 pp.4-5, 9, 11 (text layer).
rows.rationale: The SAP's conditional clause (missing-data approaches 'as required' when >15% missing at 3 months, first approach pattern-mixture plus IPW) gives partial support to the report's hierarchy, and the 3-month missingness (22.9%) met the trigger. However, the SAP never designates the pattern-mixture/IPW analysis as the primary analysis and never calls the complete-case analysis a sensitivity analysis; it calls the follow-up/MAR analysis the primary analysis. The report reverses these roles and changes the target population to all randomized. The IPW component was added on 17 July 2024, after follow-up ended in April 2024; the amendment table says it was proposed by a masked biostatistician, and Supp4 p.5 discloses it. Under the fixed review rule, disclosed changes remain differences. L substantive_difference because the primary missing-data assumption, the estimand population and the role labels differ. Card read after judgment; agrees.

rows.R: Table 2 (main p.9) HC vs PT: six cells whose RR CI includes 1 print finite positive NNT intervals, eg 24 (12-186) beside RR 1.13 (0.98-1.30). These six cells, and only these, use an en dash, and eTables 7-8 (Supp4 pp.11, 14) print the same construction with a signed NNH limit, eg 31 (13, -60). Upper limits are NNH values with the minus sign lost; implied NNH from RR limits 152, 70, 59, 39, 68, 84 vs printed 186, 76, 57, 38, 67, 79.
rows.evidence: Main p.9 (text layer incl. character codes; 200-dpi render); Supp4 pp.11, 14 (text layer); R script nnt_check.R.
rows.rationale: Footnote e says that when the RD CI contains zero the interval runs from the NNT lower limit to infinity and from an NNH (negative number) to negative infinity. Approximating the RD limits as p_PT x (RR limit - 1) from the printed painTRAINER percentage and RR CI gives NNH (from the lower RR limit) of 152, 70, 59, 39, 68, 84 and NNT (from the upper RR limit) of 10, 15, 12, 16, 10, 14, close to the printed 186/76/57/38/67/79 and 12/17/14/18/11/16. The approximation ignores the covariance between the painTRAINER percentage and the RR. The text layer shows these six cells, and only these, contain U+2013 between the limits, and the supplementary tables print such intervals as '(lower, -upper)'. So the intervals are NNT benefit x to infinity to NNH y, displayed without the minus sign. As printed they read as finite intervals excluding the null and contradict the adjacent RR intervals and the Results text (HC vs PT 'no longer significant'). Confirmed display error. Minor presentation because the RR column, footnote e and the text give the correct inference; J possible because NNT intervals may be quoted. I go beyond the card, which proposes differing RR/RD interval constructions and does not identify the lost sign.

rows.R: Table 2 (main p.9) intensity 12 mo HC vs PT prints NNT 63 (18-38). Same root cause as C008: RR 1.05 (0.92-1.20) includes 1, so the interval is NNT benefit 18 to infinity to NNH 38 with the minus sign lost (RR-based approximation: NNT 16, NNH 39). Under that reading 63 lies inside; as printed the point is outside its interval.
rows.evidence: Main p.9 (text layer and render); Supp4 pp.11, 14 for the signed convention; R script nnt_check.R.
rows.rationale: Point recomputed: 33.7 - 32.1 = 1.6 points, 100/1.6 = 62.5, ceiling 63 (see C004 for the round-up convention). Interval: the RR interval includes 1, so by footnote e the NNT set is [18, infinity) together with an NNH branch from 38; the en dash and the supplementary '(a, -b)' convention show that '38' is an NNH with a dropped sign. The printed tuple is still erroneous (a point outside its displayed interval), but it is a manifestation of the C008 display defect rather than a separate computational error. Retained so the cell-level defect is recorded; minor because the point is correct and the error is self-evident. The card does not identify this mechanism.

rows.R: Table 3 (main pp.10-11): 14 of 63 SMD points lie outside their printed 95% CIs (eg severity 12 mo PT vs UC -0.25 (-0.24 to 0.01)); 18 intervals are printed with descending limits (social, physical rows); in 20 cells the SMD CI and MD CI disagree on excluding zero (eg severity 12 mo PT vs UC MD -0.4 (-0.6 to -0.2) but SMD CI includes 0).
rows.evidence: Main pp.10-11 (text layer plus 200-dpi renders); R script smd_check.R.
rows.rationale: Recomputation (R) over all 63 SMD tuples: 14 points outside the numeric range of their limits (the card's 14 tuples match mine); 18 tuples with lower > upper; 20 tuples where significance by the SMD interval differs from significance by the MD interval of the same contrast, which cannot happen when SMD = MD/SD with SD fixed. The intervals are therefore not intervals for the printed SMDs. With C003, the whole SMD panel of Table 3 is unreliable. Substantive and direct because SMDs and their CIs are standard extraction targets and the Results text quotes them. Card read after judgment; agrees.

rows.R: Supp4 p.13 describes eTable 8 as the primary analysis restricted to subsets, but eTable 8 footnote b (p.14) lists only the base covariates (sex, age, site, residence, multisite pain, mental health, baseline severity), omitting the education and employment terms that eTable 2 (p.7) adds to the primary models. The footnote is identical to eTable 7's complete-case footnote. Report contradicts itself on the subset model.
rows.evidence: Supp4 pp.4, 7-9, 11, 13-14 (text layer).
rows.rationale: Either the subset analyses dropped the two selected covariates (and perhaps the imputation/weighting, which the footnote does not mention), so they are not 'the primary analysis' restricted to subsets, or footnote b was copied from eTable 7 and is wrong. The documents establish the contradiction but not which is true; under the Codebook definition that is a confirmed reporting issue with an unknown correct description. Minor because these are post hoc/sensitivity subsets and the estimates themselves are not shown to be wrong. Card read after judgment; agrees.

rows.R: eTable 2 (Supp4 p.7) lists education among the additional nonresponse-weight predictors; the fitted weight model, eTable 5 (p.10), has no education term but includes 'Not employed'. Workbook (Supp5 eTable 3) selection P values support employment (MCID P<.001, nonresponse P=.0228) and not education (no nonresponse P listed), so eTable 2's list appears wrong.
rows.evidence: Supp4 pp.5, 7, 10 (text layer); Supp5 xlsx sheet 'eTable 3' rows 12-18, 39, 81, 84, 108 columns H-J (openpyxl).
rows.rationale: The selection rule for the weight model (Supp4 p.5) requires P<0.10 for both the 3-month MCID model and any-follow-up model. Workbook columns H (MCID) and I (nonresponse): not employed <0.001 and 0.0228 (qualifies); education 0.0156 and blank (does not qualify on nonresponse); PEG 0.0245/0.0405, PHQ-8 <0.001/0.0095, GAD-7 0.0327/0.0331, any negative SDOH 0.0636/0.0196 (all qualify). So eTable 5's fitted set (PEG, PHQ-8, GAD-7, SDOH, not employed) follows the stated rule, and eTable 2's 'education' is a listing error. Beyond the card, which leaves the substitution unresolved, the workbook resolves the direction. Minor because the fitted model is displayed.

rows.R: eTable 2 (Supp4 p.7) specifies education as binary (any college vs HS or less), but eTables 3 and 4 (pp.8-9) fit three nonreference education terms, two of them labeled 'AA degree' (eg eTable 4 RR 0.97 and 1.16). The workbook (Supp5) has four education levels (HS or less, Associate's/technical, College, Doctoral/postgraduate), consistent with a 4-level coding and a duplicated label.
rows.evidence: Supp4 pp.7-9 (text layer); Supp5 xlsx sheet 'eTable 3' A12:A16.
rows.rationale: A binary variable yields one coefficient; three are shown in both fitted models. The workbook's four categories match three nonreference terms, so the fitted models probably used the 4-level variable and the second 'AA degree' row is most likely 'College degree'; this assignment is my inference and is not stated. The specification and the fitted displays contradict each other. Minor: nuisance covariates in supplementary model summaries. Card read after judgment; agrees.

rows.R: eTable 3 (Supp4 p.8): 7 rows have 95% CIs excluding 0 but P>.05 (eg Pattern 2 -0.28 (-0.47 to -0.08), P=.150). Printed P values reproduce almost exactly if each interval is estimate +/- 1 SE (r = 0.999 over rows with P>=.001; SE implied by P is 1.95 x the 95%-CI SE), so the 'CIs' are ~68% intervals. The three ratio rows in eTables 4-5 (age, second AA, PEG) are compatible with rounding.
rows.evidence: Supp4 pp.8-10 (text layer); R script etab3.R.
rows.rationale: Recomputation (R): for the 20 eTable 3 rows with a numeric P (excluding the 8 printed <.001), SE from P = |est|/z(1-P/2) divided by SE from the CI as a 95% interval had median 1.945; P implied by est/(half-width) reproduced printed P (eg Time 6M .030 vs .025, Pattern 2 .151 vs .150, Site 3 .070 vs .069, Male .0034 vs .003). The table's intervals are therefore est +/- 1 SE, mislabeled 95% CI; the printed P values appear right. Card rows in eTables 4 and 5: age RR 1.15 (1.00-1.33) P=.046 and second AA 1.16 (1-1.33) P=.046 give CI-implied P .055 and .042 at the printed values, and PEG 0.96 (0.92-1.00) P=.037 gives .055, all reachable within half-unit rounding (ranges include .046 and .037), so I do not count them. I retain the candidate for the seven eTable 3 rows. Minor: an imputation-model summary whose P values are correct; J unlikely. I go beyond the card, which does not identify the +/-1 SE construction and includes the three rounding-compatible ratio rows.

rows.R: eTable 8 first header (Supp4 p.14): 'N=454; 366 with at least 1 follow-up; PT=149, HC=153, UC=152 at 3-months'. 149+153+152 = 454 = N randomized, which exceeds the 366 with any follow-up, so these are not 3-month counts. By subtraction (eTable 1 minus the post-8/9/2021 header) the 3-month counts would be UC 109, PT 94, HC 108 (total 311).
rows.evidence: Supp4 pp.7, 13-14 (text layer).
rows.rationale: The other two headers give 3-month counts below their any-follow-up totals (1487 <= 1670; 858 <= 935). eTable 1 3-month completers: UC 621, PT 542, HC 635; post-enhancement block UC 512, PT 448, HC 527; differences 109, 94, 108 (sum 311 <= 366), consistent with the first block being the complement (454 + 1877 = 2331). The first header's arm counts are randomized arm sizes mislabeled as 3-month counts. Minor: denominators in a subset sensitivity table, with estimates unaffected. Card read after judgment; agrees, and I add the subtraction check.

rows.R: eTable 11 (Supp4 p.17) is titled and headed 'Raw Score Median (25%-tile, 75%-tile)' but the text (p.15) calls the values means; bounds such as 5.1 (4.9, 5.2) for a 0-10 score (baseline SD 1.6) are far too narrow for IQRs and look like 95% CIs of means. Group columns also appear to be in the order UC, PT, HC, not the labeled PT, HC, UC: printed MDs match differences under UC/PT/HC (mean abs error 0.03) but not as labeled (1.02).
rows.evidence: Supp4 pp.15, 17-18 (text layer); main Tables 1 and 3 for plausibility; R script etab11_cols.R.
rows.rationale: Recomputation (R): for all 21 rows I compared the printed between-group MDs with differences of the three summary columns under the labeled order (PT, HC, UC) and under UC, PT, HC. Mean absolute error 1.019 as labeled vs 0.032 under UC/PT/HC. Plausibility: Table 1 baseline severity about 5.8-5.9 and Table 3 adjusted 3-month change UC -0.8, PT -1.2, HC -1.2 imply 3-month means UC about 5.1, PT 4.6, HC 4.7, matching columns 1, 2, 3 = 5.1, 4.6, 4.6. Most bounds are about +/-0.1-0.6, typical of 95% CIs for means with n~600; two PGIC cells (2.0 (1.0, 3.0), 2.0 (1.0, 2.0)) look like true median/IQR, so summary types may be mixed. As labeled, a reader would assign usual-care values to painTRAINER. Substantive and direct for anyone extracting arm-level follow-up scores. Beyond the card, which documents the mean/median label conflict but not the column misassignment.

rows.R: Supp5 workbook, sheet 'eTable 3', E82: All Observed (N=1568, 2 missing per E83) current depression '711 (73.2)'. 711/1566 = 45.4%. Row reconciles otherwise: 162+243+711 = 1116 (B82), and B82 1116/2329 = 47.9%, C82 162/295 = 54.9%, D82 243/468 = 51.9% reproduce.
rows.evidence: Supp5 xlsx sheet 'eTable 3' rows 3, 82-83, 110 (openpyxl, cached values).
rows.rationale: Footnote a (A110) says missing values are excluded from the denominator. 711/(1568-2) = 45.40%. 73.2% would need a denominator of about 971. The counts sum correctly across the three missingness patterns, so the percentage alone is wrong. As printed it suggests that completers were far more depressed than noncompleters, the reverse of the true pattern (45.4% vs 51.9-54.9%). Minor because the count is right and the workbook is a descriptive supplement; J unlikely. Card read after judgment; agrees.

rows.R: eTable 11 (Supp4 p.17) physical function: 2-df Wald omnibus P reconstructed from the three contrast CIs (Cov from Var(HC-PT) = Var(a)+Var(b)-2Cov) is .025 at 6 mo and .010 at 12 mo, vs printed .005 and .001; P ranges allowing +/-0.05 display rounding are .0096-.051 and .0032-.024, excluding the printed values. The other rows are compatible. Probable because eTable 11 does not define its omnibus test.
rows.evidence: Supp4 pp.15-18 (text layer); R scripts omnibus.R, omnibus2.R (seed 20261014).
rows.rationale: If the three pairwise contrasts come from one GEE fit, the HC-PT contrast fixes the covariance of the PT-UC and HC-UC contrasts, and the 2-df Wald statistic d'V^-1 d is determined (it is also the maximum squared z over all contrasts, so it cannot be smaller than any pairwise z^2). Physical 6 mo: PT-UC 1.1 (0.3, 1.9), HC-UC 0.4 (-0.3, 1.1), HC-PT -0.6 (-1.4, 0.1): X2 = 7.34, P = .025. Physical 12 mo: X2 = 9.18, P = .010. Uniform perturbation of all nine inputs within +/-0.05 (20,000 draws, seed 20261014) gives P ranges .0096-.051 and .0032-.024, which exclude the printed .005 and .001. Physical 3 mo (printed .212, reconstructed .18) and the remaining rows are compatible; pain intensity 12 mo (printed <.001, reconstructed .020) has a range down to <.001 because of near-singular inputs. The footnote defines only the MDs, and main Table 3's footnote c describes a Wald test for the adjusted analysis, not this unadjusted table. A different omnibus procedure (eg a rank test on the raw scores) cannot be ruled out, so probable rather than confirmed. Minor: printed and reconstructed P are both below .05 at 12 months, and at 6 months the conclusion is borderline only under extreme rounding; J unlikely. Card read after judgment; it uses the same reconstruction family and agrees.

rows.R: Main p.3 describes PROMIS-29 as 7 domains (raw 4-20 each) of mixed direction, yet p.6 and eTable 4 (Supp3 p.15) report one 'PROMIS-29 score' (about 65, SD 14) and an adjusted MD of -0.37 (-3.34 to 2.61) with no aggregation, transformation or favorable direction stated; protocol p.70 describes domain T-scores (mean 50, SD 10). Also main p.6 levodopa mean 66 vs eTable 4 64.74.
rows.evidence: Main pp.3, 6 (text layer); Supp3 p.15 eTable 4 (text layer); protocol Supp1 p.70 (garbled text layer; OCR 300 dpi).
rows.rationale: PROMIS-29 has no standard single raw total: its seven 4-item domains point in opposite directions (physical function and social roles higher = better; anxiety, depression, fatigue, sleep disturbance and pain interference higher = worse), and the pain-intensity item is 0-10. The protocol frames PROMIS scales as T-scores (mean 50, SD 10). A single mean of 65 fits neither a domain T-score nor a stated composite, and the report does not say how the scalar was built or which direction favors levodopa. The adjusted difference therefore cannot be interpreted or extracted. Beyond the card, I note a copy discrepancy: main p.6 gives levodopa 66 (14) vs placebo 65 (14), while eTable 4 gives 64.74 (14.33) vs 65.11 (13.79), so the levodopa mean should round to 65 and the order of the group means is reversed. Similar copy problems affect PROMIS-10 (main 28 (6) both groups vs eTable 4 29.87/30.04). Substantive because the effect estimate of a named secondary outcome is ambiguous in scale and direction (the Codebook example); J possible because the outcome is exploratory and null. Card read after judgment; agrees.

rows.R: Protocol §11.4.1-11.4.2 (p.86) and §11.5 (p.87): primary analysis in the FAS of all randomized, missing data by multiple imputation. SAP (p.4 footnote 1; §4.3) and report (main p.4; Supp3 pp.12-13) exclude the 28 participants who died before 3 months from the primary analysis (n=582 of 610); death-inclusive analyses (estimands 3, 4; post hoc estimand 10) are supportive. Report calls the protocol-SAP differences 'terminology' (main p.5).
rows.evidence: Protocol Supp1 pp.86-87 (OCR then 120-dpi renders read); SAP Supp2 pp.4, 6-8 (no text layer; OCR 300 dpi); main pp.4-6; Supp3 pp.12-14 (text layer).
rows.rationale: Recomputed flow: 307-11 = 296, 303-17 = 286, 296+286 = 582 = 610-28. The protocol puts the primary analysis on the full analysis set of all randomized patients and handles missing data by multiple imputation, with no rule excluding deaths. The SAP (signed September 2024, before database closure) keeps deaths in the FAS label but excludes them from every analysis except treatment-policy III and the composite strategy. The report follows the SAP. The primary estimand population therefore moved from all randomized to survivors, a change of analysis population rather than of terminology as main p.5 suggests. Death-inclusive results are reported and similar (-0.98 [-3.77, 1.81], n=610; composite 1.06 [0.86, 1.26]; post hoc deaths = 0, -0.03 [-3.27, 3.21]), which bears on impact, not on whether a difference exists. Partly disclosed (main p.5 general statement). Card read after judgment; agrees.

rows.R: Every supplied protocol version specifies a mixed model with a random center intercept (synopses pp.10, 56; §11.4.2 pp.39, 86), and the final version adds stroke type as a fixed effect. SAP §5.2 (p.10), main p.4 and the code (Supp5, OCR: lm(fma_affected.Visit_3 ~ fma_affected.Visit_1.cent + medication)) fit baseline FMA and treatment only. Randomization was minimized within center (main p.3), but center is not in the analysis model.
rows.evidence: Protocol Supp1 pp.10, 39, 56, 86 (OCR, p.86 rendered); SAP Supp2 p.10 (OCR); main pp.3-5; Supp5 code (no usable text layer; OCR 300 dpi).
rows.rationale: The planned primary model contains two terms that the implemented model lacks: a random center intercept (in all supplied protocol versions) and stroke type (final protocol). The SAP, signed before database closure, already specifies the reduced linear model, so the change predates unblinding as far as the documents show; the report's statement that protocol-SAP differences concern 'statistical terminology' (main p.5) does not describe a model change. The omitted center term is also the stratification variable of the minimization (main p.3), which the plan accounted for. With a null result (-0.90, -3.78 to 1.98) the practical consequence is probably small, but the primary model differs from the protocol. Card read after judgment; agrees.

rows.R: SAP §6 (p.11): missing secondary outcomes imputed as for the primary analysis (100 MICE imputations); only harm outcomes not imputed. Report (main p.5; Supp3 p.7 deviations) did not impute mRS (deaths set to 6; analysis n=596) or the patient-reported relevance item (PRAI; n=546). Disclosed as SAP deviations in Supp3 p.7.
rows.evidence: SAP Supp2 pp.10-11 (OCR; p.11 viewed as 300-dpi image); main pp.5-6; Supp3 pp.7, 15 (text layer).
rows.rationale: mRS and PRAI are secondary efficacy outcomes, not harm outcomes, so the SAP rule requires imputation. The report analyzes observed data for both (eTable 4 n=596 for mRS and 546 for PRAI, against 582 survivors imputed for the other secondary outcomes). Assigning mRS 6 at death is defensible, but the main text says mRS missing data were not imputed at all, which is broader than the supplement's death-only explanation. Disclosed (Supp3 p.7), which under the fixed review rule is context rather than grounds for exclusion. Beyond the card: the PRAI placebo numerator is 52/270 in main p.6 but 51/270 (18.89%) in eTable 4, and Supp3 p.7 announces 'two deviations' but lists three. Card read after judgment; agrees.

rows.R: Not found in any report document (main article; Supp3 index of 9 eTables and 7 eFigures; Supp4 is the investigator list): SAP §7 center and treatment-by-center interaction model, SAP §7.2 seven prespecified subgroup interactions with forest plot (ICEMAN addendum pp.14-15), protocol §11.4.3(b) treatment x stroke type and (c) added-covariable analyses. Planned analyses reported as 'post hoc': center plot (eFigure 5) and the protocol per-protocol set (estimand 11). Main p.5 says prespecified analyses were performed as outlined in the SAP.
rows.evidence: SAP Supp2 pp.11-12, 14-15 (OCR; p.11 viewed); protocol Supp1 p.86 (rendered); main pp.4-5, 7; Supp3 pp.2, 12-14, 18, 25, 27 (text layer; eFigures 5 and 7 rendered at 110 dpi); Supp4 (text layer).
rows.rationale: I searched every supplied report document. Supp3 contains estimand analyses (eTables 2-3), a continuous baseline-FMA interaction and spline model (eTables 7-8), a center boxplot (eFigure 5) and a forest plot of post hoc analyses (eFigure 7: deaths = 0, strict adherence, and FMA <=35 vs >35). None gives the seven SAP subgroup interactions (age, sex, distal motor function, cortical dysfunction, SSRI use, stroke type, baseline FMA severity split at the median), the center-by-treatment interaction model, the protocol's treatment x stroke-type interaction or its additional-covariable models. The post hoc FMA split (<=35 vs >35) approximates the planned median split (overall median 34) but is labeled post hoc. Beyond the card: the protocol (§11.4.1, §11.4.3e) prespecifies a per-protocol analysis (>=80% medication and >=5 rehabilitation sessions per week) that the report presents as post hoc estimand 11 (n=395), and the protocol and SAP prespecify the graphical center display that main p.5 calls a post hoc exploratory plot. Under protocol_report rules, planned analyses that are absent and prespecified analyses relabeled post hoc are both differences. Card read after judgment; agrees, and I add the two relabelings.

rows.R: Table 2 (main p.6, rendered): levodopa SAE categories sum to 143 vs 126 events (placebo 139 vs 129); infection subtypes sum to 59 vs 55 (levodopa) and 52 vs 44 (placebo). Stroke and cardiac subtypes and the prespecified-AE block (79, 67) reconcile exactly. Fall, fracture and trauma rows suggest events can carry several categories, but no note says so; only stroke subtypes are indented. Cannot decide whether this is an error or unstated multiple classification.
rows.evidence: Main pp.6-7 (text layer; Table 2 rendered at 170 dpi to check indentation); Supp3 pp.16-17 eTables 5-6 (text layer).
rows.rationale: Sums (recomputed in Python): levodopa top-level rows 55+16+5+12+4+4+6+3+3+2+1+0+32 = 143; placebo 44+19+10+3+7+5+2+6+4+2+3+0+34 = 139. Infection subtypes: levodopa 27+15+5+0+1+11 = 59; placebo 17+15+7+2+2+9 = 52. Nested rows that do reconcile: stroke 15+1 = 16 and 18+1 = 19; cardiac 5+5+2 = 12 and 1+2+0 = 3; fall = trauma (4/4, 5/5). Prespecified AEs of interest sum exactly to 79 and 67. eTable 5 breakdowns (severity 103+106+46, outcome 6+76+29+0+142+2) sum to 255 = 126+129. A fracture after a fall is plausibly counted under trauma, fall and fracture at once, and an infection can involve two sites, so overlapping classification could explain all excesses (17, 10, 4 and 8 events), but the table neither states this nor separates exclusive categories, and the visual hierarchy is ambiguous. I therefore record the presentation problem with indeterminate certainty. Minor: the totals quoted in the text and the safety conclusion do not depend on the category split. Card read after judgment; it treats infection subtypes as nested by indentation, but my render shows only the stroke subtypes are indented. Also observed: eTable 6 gives overall n = 145 although 67+79 = 146 and each breakdown sums to 146.
